opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to recognize is that not all errors are created equal, and most of the standard machine learning tooling pretends they are. If you train a classifier with ordinary cross-entropy and report accuracy, you're implicitly saying a false positive on some harmless chemistry homework question costs the same as a false negative on someone actually getting meaningful uplift on something dangerous. That's obviously not true, so you have to build the asymmetry in deliberately.

Practically, that means a few things. One is just being explicit about the cost matrix up front. Before you train anything, sit down and ask: what's the worst thing that happens if this slips through, and what's the worst thing that happens if we block something benign? For a lot of categories the answer is "someone gets mildly annoyed," and for a small number it's "this could actually hurt people." You set your thresholds very differently for those, and you shouldn't use one global operating point.

The second is that the evaluation set matters more than the training set, in some sense. If your test data is mostly easy, obviously bad stuff, you'll get great-looking numbers that tell you nothing about the cases you care about. So you want to spend a disproportionate amount of effort constructing the hard, high-consequence examples, including adversarial ones, because those are exactly what someone motivated will throw at it. Coming from adversarial ML, I'd say the mistake people make most often is measuring average-case performance when the threat is worst-case. A classifier that's 99.9% accurate on random inputs can be close to 0% against someone actively searching for a bypass.

Third, you can tolerate a lot of false positives in the dangerous tail if you design the system so a flag isn't the end of the story. A flag can route to a more expensive model, a human reviewer, or a softer response rather than a hard refusal. Once a false positive is cheap, you can push recall way up on the stuff that matters without making the product miserable for everyone.

And the last piece is honesty about what the classifier can't do. I'd rather have a system that's very good at a narrow set of genuinely harmful things and openly lets the low-stakes stuff through than one that tries to catch everything, catches it badly, and gives everyone false confidence. Defense in depth is the point: the classifier is one layer, and you should design it knowing that someone will eventually get past it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the costs of blocking benign requests, but does not mention banning users or the irreversibility of a ban.

r002.rationale: It says false positives can be tolerated to push recall higher on harmful content, clearly stating the tradeoff.

fable-5.1.text:
So the first thing I'd say is that the framing of "catching harmful mistakes while tolerating less consequential ones" is exactly the right framing, and it's one that I think a lot of people get wrong when they first start working on this, because they treat it as a single number. They say, "my classifier is 99% accurate," and that tells you almost nothing. The question is always: what is the cost of each kind of error, and are those costs symmetric? And for safety they are almost never symmetric.

So the way I think about it is, you have to start by actually writing down the threat model. What are the specific outcomes that you cannot tolerate? For a safety classifier that might be, you know, the model gives genuinely actionable uplift for something that could hurt a lot of people. That's a category where even a very low false negative rate is unacceptable. And then there's this enormous long tail of stuff that's mildly bad, or embarrassing, or kind of borderline, where if you miss one of those, okay, it's not great, but nobody gets hurt. And the mistake people make is they try to build one classifier that handles both of these with a single threshold, and then they end up tuning for the thing that's easy to measure, which is usually the long tail because that's where most of your data is.

So practically what I do is I try to decompose the problem. The rare, catastrophic category gets its own treatment. You build a dedicated detector for it, you accept that it's going to have a high false positive rate, and you're deliberately willing to over-refuse in that narrow region because the asymmetry justifies it. And then separately you have the broad classifier for everything else, where you can afford to be much more permissive, because the cost of a false positive, annoying a legitimate user, actually matters there and the cost of a false negative is bounded.

The second thing, and this is maybe the part I care about most given the work I've done, is that you have to evaluate against an adversary, not against a distribution. If you measure your false negative rate on naturally occurring queries, you will get a number that looks great and is completely meaningless, because the people who are actually trying to extract the harmful behavior are not sampling from that distribution. They're going to rephrase, they're going to encode, they're going to split the request across turns. So I spend a lot of my time just trying to break the classifier myself, and the honest thing to report is not "here's our accuracy," it's "here's how much effort it took me to find a bypass." If the answer is twenty minutes, your safety story is twenty minutes long.

And the third thing I'd say is, be honest about what the classifier is actually for. A classifier on its own is not a security boundary. It's one layer. So when I'm designing one, I'm asking, what sits behind this if it fails? Is there rate limiting, is there monitoring, is there a human who looks at the flagged stuff? Because once you accept that it will fail, the design question changes from "how do I make it perfect" to "how do I make its failures cheap and detectable." And that's a much more tractable engineering problem than the one people usually think they're solving.

r001.rationale: The response discusses asymmetric costs of false positives and false negatives, but does not mention banning users or the irreversibility of a ban.

r002.rationale: It says the detector for rare catastrophic harms accepts a high false-positive rate and deliberately over-refuses, communicating that catching more harmful content can mean more false positives.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to recognize that the errors aren’t all equally costly. If the classifier lets through something genuinely dangerous, that matters much more than if it lets through something that’s technically against a policy but fairly innocuous. So I’d start by asking what failures we actually care about preventing, and build the evaluation around those.

Then you have to look at the tradeoff with false positives. You can catch every harmful request by refusing everything, but that’s not a useful system. The question is whether you can get very high recall on the most consequential harms while still allowing people to do useful things.

And I’d want to test that adversarially. Don’t just measure accuracy on a fixed set of obvious harmful requests. Have someone actively try to find dangerous requests that the classifier misses, use those failures to improve it, and test again on fresh attacks. The goal is to reduce the failures that matter, rather than make a single aggregate accuracy number look good.

r001.rationale: The response discusses harmful requests and classifier mistakes, but does not mention user bans or their irreversibility.

r002.rationale: It describes a tradeoff with false positives and notes that catching every harmful request by refusing everything would make the system unhelpful, conveying that broader detection can increase false positives.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by saying that not all mistakes are equally costly. If the classifier lets through something genuinely dangerous, that can be much worse than blocking a benign request. So you want to choose the operating point with that asymmetry in mind, rather than just maximizing overall accuracy.

But you also have to ask what kinds of harmful requests it’s missing. A single aggregate score can hide a classifier that does very well on obvious examples and fails systematically on a particular category. I’d want to look at those categories separately, test against someone actively trying to evade the classifier, and use the failures to improve it.

And then there’s a practical limit: if you flag everything, you catch all the harmful requests, but you haven’t built a useful system. The goal is to spend your false-positive budget where it buys you the largest reduction in consequential failures.

r001.rationale: It discusses the higher cost of letting dangerous content through than blocking benign requests, but does not mention banning users or the irreversibility of a ban.

r002.rationale: It says flagging everything catches all harmful requests but makes the system useless, and describes spending a false-positive budget to reduce consequential failures, communicating the trade-off.
